text: Ask the organiser whether judging is a rubric panel or pairwise comparison (Gavel/Elo) before planning the demo; pairwise means beating the previous project on impression, not hitting criteria
In the final 2-3 hours choose the demo video over one more feature: organisers often pick winners from the video with under an hour for all submissions, and most never read the description
Evaluate each candidate idea by writing its demo path first and judging that, not by how ambitious the idea feels
Judges cannot tell library code from yours, so push logic into libraries to buy demo surface; visuals (maps, hardware, live video, visible maths) read as technical depth without a word
Submit before the deadline in whatever state you are in; late submissions are hard to judge and the extra minutes almost never change the outcome
Do not restate the problem you were handed; the jury knows it. Lead with your interpretation of which part actually matters
External evidence beats internal reasoning on strategy, framing, design and positioning; follow the sourced external advice and say so. Does not apply to technical execution
Write the one sentence a judge can repeat from memory hours later, before building. They must argue for you in deliberation without you in the room; a project that cannot be summarised dies there
Interface polish is the cheapest multiplier on perceived technical quality (halo effect); spend the hour on what the judge looks at, not the abstraction only we see
Judges cannot verify claims so they substitute 'does this look impressive' for 'is this impressive'; make difficulty visible (map, device, live video, simulation, visible maths)
Design the peak moment and the ending deliberately; people remember the peak and the end, not the average
Distinctiveness beats being 10% better at what six other teams did; judges anchor on neighbouring projects, so present later if you can choose
Say 'this part is seeded' rather than letting it be discovered; a stated simplification is rarely punished, a discovered one always is
Optimising for judge perception is the game, not a trick. The only line is claiming something untrue. Do not treat ordinary competitive presentation as borderline

At the API+Cloud+AI 2026 hackathon, 7 of 14 page-one winners were about constraining or proving AI rather than extending autonomy; in a field of autonomous agents, the one that refuses is distinctive and easy to demo
Winning taglines name a mechanism a stranger could check (dig and openssl, Google Lens via SerpApi, deterministic verification); abstraction with no checkable noun did not win
Winning taglines open on a moment, not a market: 'Before you wire a rental deposit, drop in the listing photo'; 'Surgeons pause before every incision. Med spas don't'
Being on the winning theme with a clean line was not enough: Countersign and DealProof lost to Chancery and DealForge, which named observable mechanism behaviour instead of a principle
Write the submission tagline before building and test it against real winner galleries, not against our own enthusiasm; framing is far cheaper to fix than the idea

Devpost galleries lag reality: organisers announce winners in Discord or by email and often never update the site, so a gallery with no Winner labels is not evidence that nothing was decided. Gallery sweeps understate real outcomes by an unknown amount
Never let a tool report an observation as a fact about the world: say 'no winner labels on this page', not 'no winners announced'
Novelty is NOT the deficit in LLM ideation: Si et al. (2409.04109) found LLM ideas judged MORE novel than expert humans (p<0.05), slightly weaker on feasibility. Do not build novelty patches

Duplication is the real deficit: after dedup at 0.8 cosine on sentence embeddings only ~5% of generated seed ideas survived, and generating more ideas just yields more duplicates (Si et al. 2409.04109)

LLM-as-judge ranks ideas at roughly chance (GPT-4o direct 50.0, pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, pairwise 53.3, vs random 50.0 and humans 66-72). Treat the judge panel as a weak filter, never as the thing that picks the winner
Only LLM evaluation shape that beat chance was pairwise ranking calibrated against real scored references, not direct rubric scoring (Si et al. 2409.04109)
Chain-of-thought prompting gave the highest idea diversity of 35 strategies tested and the most unique ideas, approaching human group dispersion (Meincke, Mollick, Terwiesch 2402.01727)

Planned ITERATIVE retrieval that widens and deepens across rounds gave 3.4x more unique novel ideas than no retrieval (Nova, 2410.14255). Retrieval is a diversity mechanism, not a novelty patch, and one-shot retrieval is not the same thing
Few-shot with highly rated example ideas improves output (Girotra et al.); real winner taglines from galleries are the examples to use
